items.stem: A 14-month-old has intermittent severe colicky abdominal pain with vomiting and later passes a currant-jelly stool. Ultrasound confirms ileocolic intussusception without perforation. Which intervention is the priority nonoperative treatment for the most common type?

options.text: Arrange prompt air (pneumatic) enema reduction for ileocolic intussusception, with surgical consultation available if reduction fails or complications develop.
Discharge home with oral antacids and a high-fibre diet as the only therapy.
Start routine outpatient acupuncture and delay imaging follow-up for 2 weeks.
Give a single dose of oral castor oil and advise watchful waiting without reduction.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck states treatment is with an air enema for the most common (ileocolic) type and sometimes surgery. StatPearls notes enema reduction confirms and treats most pediatric cases (>80% success) with surgery if unsuccessful.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Antacids and diet do not reduce telescoped bowel or prevent ischemia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Delayed care risks ischemia, gangrene, and perforation.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Laxatives are not treatment for intussusception and may worsen injury.

items.stem: During a vaginal birth, the fetal head delivers then retracts (turtle sign) and the anterior shoulder will not deliver with gentle downward traction. Which nursing action is correct while assisting the provider?

options.text: Call for help, flex the client’s thighs toward the abdomen (McRoberts), and apply ordered posterolateral suprapubic pressure — avoid fundal pressure.
Apply firm continuous fundal pressure as the first and only maneuver.
Leave the room to complete charting before summoning assistance.
Place the client in Trendelenburg and pull hard on the fetal head alone.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck lists McRoberts and suprapubic pressure among initial maneuvers after announcing dystocia and calling for help. OpenStax: McRoberts then posterolateral suprapubic pressure; the nurse does not give fundal pressure because it further impacts the shoulder.
rationales.B: Incorrect. OpenStax states fundal pressure impacts the shoulder further and is not used.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate help and maneuvers.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Traction alone without proper maneuvers risks brachial plexus injury; Merck warns against relying on gentle downward traction alone once dystocia is diagnosed.

items.stem: Several household members develop headache, nausea, and confusion after using a poorly vented heater indoors. Carboxyhemoglobin is elevated. Complete the bowtie: priority condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning with elevated carboxyhemoglobin
Uncomplicated seasonal allergic rhinitis without systemic symptoms
Localized contact dermatitis from laundry detergent
Mild cerumen impaction without neurologic change

actions.text: Remove the client from the CO source and give high-flow 100% oxygen (e.g., nonrebreather) as ordered
Support airway/breathing and prepare for higher-level care (e.g., hyperbaric consult) if severe neurologic or cardiac findings
Return the client to the unventilated heater room without oxygen
Withhold all oxygen and advise outdoor jogging as sole therapy
Apply topical antifungal cream as the only intervention

parameters.text: Neurologic status (alertness, headache, confusion) and vital signs including oxygenation/cardiac status
Carboxyhemoglobin trend and response to oxygen therapy

rationales.K1: Correct. Headache, nausea, confusion with shared indoor heater exposure and elevated COHb indicate CO poisoning (Merck; StatPearls).
rationales.K2: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis does not elevate carboxyhemoglobin.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Contact dermatitis does not explain systemic CO toxicity.
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Cerumen impaction is unrelated to COHb elevation.
rationales.A1: Correct. Merck and StatPearls: remove from source and give 100% oxygen (nonrebreather).
rationales.A2: Correct. Severe cases may need advanced airway/ventilatory support; hyperbaric oxygen is considered for severe neurologic/cardiac findings (both sources).
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Continued exposure without oxygen worsens toxicity.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Oxygen therapy is first-line; withholding oxygen is unsafe.
rationales.A5: Incorrect. Antifungals do not treat CO poisoning.
rationales.P1: Correct. Neurologic and cardiopulmonary status guide severity and response (Merck symptoms; StatPearls monitoring).
rationales.P2: Correct. COHb and clinical response to oxygen track clearance (both sources).

items.stem: A community health nurse teaches a family about preventing carbon monoxide poisoning at home. Which teaching point is the priority primary-prevention action?

options.text: Install and maintain functional carbon monoxide detectors, ensure fuel-burning appliances are correctly vented outdoors, and never run a car or generator in an enclosed space such as a garage.
Disable all smoke and CO alarms to avoid false alerts.
Idle the car overnight in a closed garage during cold weather for warmth.
Place a charcoal grill inside the bedroom for overnight heating.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: install CO detectors; correctly vent indoor combustion; never leave cars running in enclosed garages. StatPearls: educate on installing functional CO detectors; never use generators/alternative heaters in enclosed spaces.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Detectors provide early warning; disabling them increases harm risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Running a car in an enclosed garage is a classic CO source (Merck).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Indoor charcoal combustion produces CO and is unsafe.

items.stem: Complete the teaching points for magnesium sulfate used in preeclampsia with severe features.

ngn.template: Intravenous magnesium sulfate is given primarily to {B1}. If significant magnesium toxicity develops (e.g., loss of reflexes with respiratory depression), the ordered antidote is typically {B2}.

B1.text: cure preeclampsia so delivery is never needed

B2.text: intravenous calcium gluconate (or calcium chloride) as ordered

rationales.B1a: Correct. Merck: magnesium sulfate prevents seizures in severe preeclampsia and treats eclampsia. OpenStax: magnesium sulfate is started to prevent progression to seizures.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Delivery is definitive treatment for preeclampsia; magnesium does not cure the disease.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Magnesium sulfate is not a vaccine substitute.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Not indicated as monotherapy for bacterial meningitis.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Merck: treat significant toxicity with calcium gluconate 1 g IV. OpenStax Pharmacology: treatment for magnesium toxicity is IV calcium gluconate or calcium chloride.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Iron does not reverse magnesium toxicity.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Vitamin C gummies are not the antidote.

items.stem: A nurse identifies a wrong-patient safety concern during a procedure timeout. The nurse states the concern clearly, but the team continues without acknowledging it. What is the priority next action?

options.text: Restate the concern assertively (two-challenge), and if it remains unresolved, escalate by engaging another team member or going up the chain of command before the unsafe action proceeds.
Remain silent to avoid conflict and allow the procedure to continue unchanged.
Leave the unit permanently without notifying anyone.
Delete the timeout checklist so the discrepancy cannot be reviewed.

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ PSNet describes the Two-Challenge Rule: state the concern, restate if not resolved, then escalate to other team members or the chain of command. OpenStax advises following the agency chain of command when seeking advice/notifications.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Silence allows a preventable never-event risk to continue.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Abandonment without escalation does not protect the client.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Destroying safety documentation worsens system learning and accountability.

items.stem: An older adult is hospitalized with a hip fracture and limited mobility. Which complication should the nurse prioritize teaching and monitoring for as the most common fatal complication of serious hip or pelvic fractures?

options.text: Pulmonary embolism related to vascular injury and immobilization — monitor for sudden dyspnea, chest pain, or oxygen desaturation and support ordered VTE prevention.
Isolated mild seasonal allergic rhinitis as the leading fatal risk.
Benign hangnail infection as the primary life-threatening complication.
Tooth enamel staining unrelated to mobility as the main fatal risk.

rationales.B: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis is not the leading fatal fracture complication.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hangnails are not life-threatening in this context.

items.stem: A client on lithium develops coarse tremor, persistent vomiting, and new confusion. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.text: Hold further lithium doses, notify the provider immediately, and closely monitor vital signs and neurologic status while awaiting ordered lithium level and management.
Double the next lithium dose to overcome the symptoms.
Encourage the client to take extra NSAIDs and a thiazide diuretic without review.
Ignore the findings because mild fine tremor always means toxicity is impossible.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: for suspected lithium toxicity, stop lithium, notify the provider, and monitor closely. Merck describes acute toxicity with gross tremor, vomiting, and confusion that can progress to seizures/arrhythmias.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Increasing the dose worsens toxicity.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Merck: NSAIDs (other than aspirin) and thiazide diuretics can contribute to hyperlithemia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Coarse tremor with vomiting/confusion indicates possible toxicity, not a benign finding.

items.stem: A client stabilized on lithium asks which new medications require extra caution because they may raise lithium levels. Select all that apply.

options.text: Thiazide diuretics
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) other than aspirin
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors
Topical sunscreen used only on intact skin
Ordinary oral rehydration with consistent salt intake as previously taught
Acetaminophen used occasionally for mild headache if otherwise appropriate

rationales.A: Correct. Merck and OpenStax: thiazide diuretics can contribute to elevated lithium levels.
rationales.B: Correct. Merck: NSAIDs other than aspirin may contribute to hyperlithemia; OpenStax lists NSAIDs as interacting.
rationales.C: Correct. Both sources list ACE inhibitors among drugs that can raise lithium levels.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Topical sunscreen on intact skin is not identified as a lithium-elevating interaction in these sources.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Consistent hydration/salt as taught supports stability; this is not a hyperlithemia-causing drug.
rationales.F: Incorrect. Acetaminophen is not listed like NSAIDs as a classic lithium-elevating interaction in these citations.

items.stem: A client at 34 weeks’ gestation is hospitalized with preeclampsia with severe features. Which medication purpose should the nurse emphasize when intravenous magnesium sulfate is ordered?

options.text: To prevent eclamptic seizures while plans for monitoring and timed delivery proceed.
To permanently dissolve all placental tissue so pregnancy continues indefinitely without delivery.
To replace the need for blood pressure assessment forever.
To treat iron-deficiency anemia as the sole indication.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: in preeclampsia with severe features, magnesium sulfate is given to prevent seizures. OpenStax: magnesium sulfate is started to prevent progression to seizures.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delivery remains definitive treatment; magnesium does not dissolve the placenta or eliminate need for delivery decisions.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Magnesium sulfate is not treatment for iron-deficiency anemia.

items.stem: Which teaching point best reflects why community-dwelling older adults need proactive protection from cold indoor environments?

options.text: Older adults are at higher risk for hypothermia because of diminished temperature sensation, impaired mobility/communication, and less subcutaneous fat — even in cool indoor rooms — so keep living spaces adequately warm and address mobility limits.
Older adults never develop hypothermia indoors under any circumstances.
Only infants can lose heat; adults are immune to cold injury.
Hypothermia occurs only after immersion in tropical swimming pools above 30°C.

rationales.A: Correct. Merck: older adults are at high risk due to diminished temperature sensation, impaired mobility/communication, and diminished subcutaneous fat; hypothermia can occur indoors in cool rooms. OpenStax links impaired thermoregulation to hypothermia risk and notes older-adult environmental vulnerabilities.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Merck explicitly notes indoor hypothermia risk for older adults.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Both age extremes are at risk (Merck).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Cool environments and impaired heat conservation drive hypothermia; tropical warm water is not the defining scenario.
